title: The thermostat that guessed
scenario: A smart-home app lets logged-in users control their heating by chat. The model has 34 tools. The logs show three repeating failures: the model calls the vague `update` tool for almost every request, it sends heating calls with both `on` and `off` set to true, and it sends temperatures like "warm". You review two of the tool definitions (exhibit). The user's household id is always known from the login session.
exhibit:
TOOL 1
name: update
description: Updates stuff.
parameters:
  user:  string
  mode:  string
  value: string

TOOL 2
name: set_heating
description: Sets heating.
parameters:
  household_id: string   (required)
  on:           boolean  (required)
  off:          boolean  (required)
  temp:         string   (required)

LOG SAMPLE
set_heating(household_id="H-2207", on=true, off=true, temp="warm")

questions.prompt: The model keeps picking `update` for heating requests. What change would help most?

options.text: Rename `update` to `UPDATE_ANYTHING` so the model notices it is generic.
options.explanation: A louder name still says nothing about when to use it. The model needs to know what the tool does and when not to use it.

options.text: Rewrite the descriptions: what each tool does, when to use it and when not.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs call detailed descriptions by far the most important factor in tool performance, and suggest at least 3–4 sentences.

options.text: Add a line to the system prompt: "Choose tools carefully."
options.explanation: That gives no new information. The model still cannot tell the two tools apart from "Updates stuff" and "Sets heating".

options.text: Move `update` to the end of the tools list so the model reads the specific tools first and prefers them.
options.explanation: Moving it does not touch the real problem: "Updates stuff" tells the model nothing about when to use the tool.

questions.prompt: How should the `on` and `off` fields be fixed?

options.text: Keep both and tell the model in the description that they must never both be true.
options.explanation: That asks the model to avoid a state the schema still allows. The advice in the OpenAI docs is to change the schema so the state cannot exist.

options.text: Keep both and reject the call in your backend when both are true.
options.explanation: Gemini does advise validating calls before you run them, but the schema still invites the mistake. Fix the schema too.

options.text: Make both fields optional so the model can leave one out.
options.explanation: Then the model can send neither, or still send both. The invalid states remain.

options.text: Replace them with one `state` field, an enum of "on" and "off".
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say to use enums and object structure to prevent invalid states, and use this same light-switch example.

options.text: Remove it from the schema and add it in your code from the login session.
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say not to make the model fill arguments you already know, and to pass them in your own code.

options.text: Keep it, and add an example id to the description so the model always uses the right format.
options.explanation: A clear format does not remove the problem: the model is still asked for a value your app already has.

options.text: Keep it, but make it optional so the model can skip it.
options.explanation: The value is still in the model's hands whenever it fills it in. Your code knows it, so your code should set it.

options.text: Rename it to `user` so it matches the `update` tool.
options.explanation: Anthropic's engineering post advises the opposite direction: specific names like `user_id`, not vague ones like `user`.

questions.prompt: Temperatures arrive as "warm" and "21C". What fix fits the vendor guidance?

options.text: Parse every string with a regex in the backend and guess the closest number when parsing fails.
options.explanation: Guessing in code hides the problem. The schema should only allow the shape you can use.

options.text: Ask the model in the system prompt to always use numbers.
options.explanation: A prompt rule helps but is still best effort. A typed schema with strict mode enforces it.

options.text: Type `temp` as an integer, describe the unit and range, and turn on strict mode.
options.explanation: Right. The Gemini docs advise specific types like integer. Claude's strict mode guarantees inputs match the schema, as in its "2" vs 2 example.

options.text: Remove `temp` and always set the heating to 20 degrees.
options.explanation: That drops a feature users need. The fix is a precise input type, not a smaller product.
